intro: Complex numbers add a new number, i, whose square is minus 1, so that every squared equation has solutions. A complex number has an ordinary part and an i part, like 3 + 2i, and can be pictured as a point on a flat map; this branch covers calculating with them and what they mean geometrically.

IV.8.01.what: Meeting the imaginary number i, defined so that i times i equals minus 1.

levels.a: Uses the rule that i squared is minus 1 to simplify.
levels.b: Explains why i was invented: to solve equations like x squared equals minus 1.
levels.c: Sees that powers of i repeat in a cycle of four: i, minus 1, minus i, 1.
levels.d: Simplifies a large power of i using that cycle.
levels.e: Adds a long list of powers of i, using the fact that each group of four cancels.
levels.f: Multiplies a long chain of powers of i, or adds them with weights.

IV.8.02.what: Taking square roots of negative numbers by writing them with i, such as the root of minus 100 equals 10i.

levels.a: Writes the square root of a negative number using i.
levels.c: Avoids the trap of combining two negative roots into one before using i.
levels.d: Multiplies roots of negatives correctly, converting to i first.

IV.8.03.what: Writing complex numbers in the standard way: an ordinary (real) part plus an imaginary part, like 6 + 6i.

levels.a: Names the real part and the imaginary part of a complex number.
levels.b: Uses the fact that two complex numbers are equal only if both parts match.
levels.c: Rewrites a complex expression in standard form.
levels.d: Classifies numbers as real, purely imaginary, or neither.

IV.8.04.what: Adding and subtracting complex numbers by combining the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

levels.b: Adds both the real and imaginary parts.
levels.c: Subtracts, applying the minus sign to both parts.
levels.d: Pictures addition as joining arrows on the complex plane.
levels.e: Solves a simple equation for an unknown complex number.
levels.f: Finds every possible fourth corner of a parallelogram from three corners.

IV.8.05.what: Multiplying complex numbers, using i squared equals minus 1 to tidy the answer.

levels.a: Multiplies a complex number by an ordinary number.
levels.b: Multiplies a complex number by i.
levels.c: Multiplies two complex numbers like two brackets, then replaces i squared by minus 1.
levels.e: Finds a value that makes a product purely real or purely imaginary.
levels.f: Finds the square roots of a complex number by matching the two parts.

IV.8.06.what: Using the conjugate of a complex number: the same number with the sign of its i part flipped.

levels.a: Writes the conjugate of a complex number.
levels.b: Multiplies a number by its conjugate, getting an ordinary real number.
levels.c: Sees the conjugate as a mirror image across the horizontal axis.
levels.d: Knows that non-real solutions of real equations come in conjugate pairs.

IV.8.07.what: Dividing complex numbers by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate, so the bottom becomes an ordinary number.

levels.a: Multiplies the top of the fraction by the conjugate of the bottom.
levels.b: Simplifies the bottom into an ordinary number.
levels.c: Gives the final answer in standard form.
levels.d: Finds one divided by a complex number.

IV.8.08.what: Picturing complex numbers as points on a flat map, with real numbers across and imaginary numbers up.

levels.a: Knows the horizontal axis holds real numbers and the vertical axis holds imaginary ones.
levels.b: Plots a complex number as a point.
levels.c: Reads the complex number at a plotted point.
levels.d: Sees adding a complex number as a move across and up.

IV.8.09.what: Finding the modulus of a complex number: its distance from zero on the complex plane.

levels.a: Uses the right-triangle rule to find the modulus.
levels.b: Sees the modulus as the distance from zero.
levels.c: Finds the distance between two complex numbers.
levels.d: Finds the point halfway between two complex numbers.
levels.e: Finds a missing part from a given distance.
levels.f: Finds the nearest and farthest a point on a circle can be from another point.

IV.8.10.what: Solving quadratics whose answers are complex numbers, when the graph never crosses the x-axis.

levels.a: Recognizes a negative value under the root means non-real answers.
levels.b: Uses the quadratic formula to find complex answers.
levels.c: Sees that the answers come as a conjugate pair.
levels.d: Checks a complex answer by putting it back in.

IV.8.11.what: The fundamental theorem of algebra: a polynomial with highest power n has exactly n roots, once complex numbers are allowed.

levels.a: States how many roots a polynomial has from its highest power.
levels.b: Counts repeated roots the right number of times.
levels.c: Uses the rule that non-real roots come in conjugate pairs.
levels.d: Builds a polynomial from its given roots.

IV.8.12.what: Writing a complex number in polar form, by its distance from zero and its angle, like giving a direction and a distance.

levels.a: Finds the angle a complex number makes with the positive real axis.
levels.b: Recognizes a number written using its distance and angle.
levels.c: Converts a standard complex number into distance-and-angle form.
levels.d: Converts distance-and-angle form back to standard form.

IV.8.13.what: Multiplying and dividing complex numbers in polar form, where distances multiply and angles add.

levels.c: Divides the distances and subtracts the angles when dividing.
levels.d: Sees multiplying as rotating and stretching.
levels.e: Finds the missing number from a product.
levels.f: Adds up many angles to find where a long chain of turns ends up.

IV.8.14.what: De Moivre's theorem: raising a complex number to a power multiplies its angle, making big powers easy.

levels.a: Raises a number in polar form to a power by multiplying the angle.
levels.b: Finds the distance and angle of a large power.
levels.c: Converts the answer back into standard form.
levels.d: Uses the theorem to find the sine or cosine of double or triple an angle.
levels.e: Finds the smallest power that makes a complex number purely real or imaginary.
levels.f: Works out a huge power of z plus one over z using the angle pattern.

IV.8.15.what: Finding all the roots of a complex number, such as its three cube roots, which are evenly spread around a circle.

levels.a: Knows there are exactly n different nth roots.
levels.b: Uses the formula that spaces the roots by equal angles.
levels.c: Finds the roots of 1, which lie evenly around a circle.
levels.d: Sees the roots as the corners of a regular polygon.
levels.e: Finds all the roots from just one of them.
levels.f: Finds the product or sum of all the roots at once.

IV.8.16.what: Describing shapes on the complex plane, such as circles and lines, using distance and angle conditions on z.

levels.a: Recognizes a fixed distance from a point as a circle, and finds its center and radius.
levels.b: Recognizes equal distances from two points as a straight line between them.
levels.c: Recognizes a fixed angle from a point as a half-line.
levels.d: Shades regions such as the inside of a circle.
levels.e: Takes out a number first to find the true center and radius.
levels.f: Finds a circle hidden in a condition where one distance is twice another.
